content: 1. The sensitivity and specificity of various rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for bacterial meningitis were compared to the gold standard methods of culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The population studied included suspected cases of bacterial meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis serogroups A, C, W, X, Y, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae type b. The outcome measured was the accuracy of RDTs in guiding the correct choice of vaccines. 2. In meningococcal meningitis outbreaks caused by Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A (NmA) before the introduction of the MenAfriVac vaccine, the proportion of cases receiving inappropriate treatment was compared to outbreaks caused by other serogroups (NmC, W, X) or NmA after MenAfriVac introduction. The intervention involved single-dose antibiotics, and the outcome was the number of cases receiving inappropriate antibiotic treatment. 3. Among household contacts of meningococcal meningitis cases, the risk of developing meningococcal meningitis within one month after disease onset was assessed. This was compared between those who received prophylaxis and those who did not. The outcome measured was the attack rate among household contacts. 4. Members of the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group completed the WHO Declaration of Interest (DoI) forms. Several declarations were made: J.M. from EHESP French School of Public Health received research support from Pfizer for a study on pneumococcal invasive disease surveillance in Togo. G.E. from PATH worked on the Meningitis Vaccine Project. R.K. from UNICEF declared travel costs paid by UNICEF. J.M.C. from the Institute of Public Health, Brussels, declared funding from Sanofi-Pasteur for work at CERMES without any patents or marketed products to declare. C.T. from the University of Cambridge received consultancy payments from GSK for evaluating health economic models and advising on vaccine carriage data. T.C. from CDC received a grant from the Gates Foundation for meningitis surveillance capacity-building in sub-Saharan Africa. M.L.F. from Serum Institute of India declared employment and involvement in the Meningitis Vaccine Project. D.S. from Emory University served as an unpaid advisor for MenAfriCar and other meningitis-related projects. B.M.G. from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine received research grants from the Wellcome Trust and Gates Foundation. M.H. from Médecins Sans Frontières presented MSF’s opinions on meningitis in WHO-organized meetings. B.D.G. from Agence de Médecine Préventive declared funding from various vaccine manufacturers and organizations, including the Gates Foundation and GAVI. 5. The GRADE evidence profiles evaluated the performance of RDTs for meningitis in outbreak management. For Neisseria meningitidis serogroup W: Under field conditions, pooled sensitivity was 92% (95% CI: 88–94%), and specificity was 95% (95% CI: 93–96%). Under laboratory conditions, pooled sensitivity was 97% (95% CI: 95–98%), and specificity was 95% (95% CI: 93–96%). 6. For Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A: Under field conditions, sensitivity was 87% (95% CI: 84–89%), and specificity was 79% (95% CI: 76–82%). Under laboratory conditions, sensitivity was 86% (95% CI: 84–89%), and specificity was 77% (95% CI: 74–79%). 7. The Pastorex test for Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A under field conditions showed sensitivity of 65% (95% CI: 53–75%) and specificity of 84% (95% CI: 72–92%). However, the confidence intervals were wide, indicating uncertainty in the estimates. 8. The BinaxNOW test for Streptococcus pneumoniae under laboratory conditions demonstrated pooled sensitivity of 99% (95% CI: 96–100%) and specificity of 96% (95% CI: 95–97%). 9. The use of chemoprophylaxis to prevent meningococcal disease among household contacts was evaluated. The evidence quality was very low due to serious limitations, including high risk of bias and lack of adjustment for confounding factors. Resistance to antibiotics, except rifampicin, was not detected. 10. The use of vaccination to prevent meningococcal disease among household contacts was assessed. The evidence quality was very low due to unclear risks of bias and insufficient sample sizes. 11. The combined use of chemoprophylaxis and vaccination for household contacts was also evaluated, but the evidence quality remained very low due to similar limitations.
